tagline: An inland road winding past lakes and mountains toward Cherryfield
intro: Blackwoods follows inland Route 182 through forest, winding past Fox Pond, Spring River Lake and Tunk Lake, with Tunk and Catherine mountains along the way. The National Scenic Byway Foundation lists it as a state byway and describes a quiet, two-lane road with blueberry barrens and historic architecture in its gateway towns, Franklin and Cherryfield.

Earlier journeys left a tangible object beside Route 182 in Franklin: the Robertson Quarry Galamander, a specialized wagon for hauling stone. Recovered from a local quarry in 1965, it is displayed beneath a shelter with panels explaining its use. Its derrick lifted stone slabs onto and off the wagon.

From Franklin, the road curves east into unorganized East Hancock and winds among the lakes and mountains before houses reappear in Cherryfield. There, it crosses the rail trail and sweeps south, bypassing an older alignment closer to the Narraguagus River. Route 182 ends at US 1 just west of the river and town center.

moments.title: Catherine's Hill
moments.text: Catherine’s Hill names a rise in Black’s Woods Road near Catherine Mountain, ending a short distance from Fox Pond. The mountain reaches 962 feet; its namesake belongs to local legend. In the ghost story, travelers describe a woman asking for a ride, sometimes to Bar Harbor, and Catherine is said to wear a light blue gown. Versions differ: some tell of an accident, others of a witch or a girl lost to supernatural forces.

moments.title: Narraguagus River
moments.text: The Narraguagus flows through Cherryfield on its way to a mouth in Milbridge. Atlantic salmon once brought fly anglers here from far away for the Memorial Day weekend opening. The native salmon run has since been much reduced, a change the source attributes to multiple factors without identifying them.

moments.title: Cherryfield
moments.text: Cherryfield’s wooden houses include a concentration of Second Empire designs on both sides of the Narraguagus River. One example, the William M. Nash House, changed from a Cape to a Greek Revival house before William Nash commissioned its Second Empire redesign in 1888. Its mansard roof provides a full third floor, and a tower projects from the front. The historic district records the 19th-century development of a riverside community through its houses and commercial buildings.
moments.notice: The Nash House combines a mansard roof with a projecting front tower.
